source.title: Memorization and Optimization in Deep Neural Networks with Minimum Over-parameterization
source.authors: Simone Bombari; Mohammad Hossein Amani; Marco Mondelli

record.file_problem: none; supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: Its theoretical memorization result applies to arbitrary real-valued labels and its gradient-descent result proves convergence under a specially constructed initialization. The small experiments assess NTK eigenvalues and loss, rather than reproducing the original random-image-label experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work reporting that roughly 10^6 parameters suffice to fit random CIFAR-10 labels and 2.4·10^7 parameters suffice for a subset of ImageNet, but these are not this study's results. Its own memorization theorem covers arbitrary real-valued labels but does not report random-label test error or image-label experiments. The loss plot uses Gaussian inputs and Gaussian targets and Adam; it is not a random-label experiment.
record.test_reason: The gradient-descent theorem guarantees fitting arbitrary labels, including random labels, under explicit assumptions. The illustrative experiment also reports zero loss on Gaussian inputs and Gaussian targets, directly bearing on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors establish NTK conditioning, memorization capacity and gradient-descent convergence with nearly minimal over-parameterization. The theoretical results require smooth activations and loose pyramidal topology; the optimization guarantee additionally uses a specially constructed initialization. They regard the activation and topology restrictions as technical and leave their removal open.
record.recipe_differences: The main results are theoretical NTK and memorization-capacity guarantees. The optimization theorem uses a specially designed duplicated-neuron initialization and boosted final-layer variance; the illustrative experiment uses Adam. This is not the original empirical random-label fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The optimization guarantee depends on the specially constructed initialization and the learning-rate bound. The paper's main theorem assumes smooth activations and loose pyramidal topology; its illustrative loss experiment uses ReLU and Adam.

fits_no_version.finding: Networks can represent arbitrary real-valued training targets to arbitrarily small error under the corollary's assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep networks with nearly linear parameter count have sufficient representational capacity to memorize arbitrary targets, independently of whether a specified training algorithm finds them.

record.problems: The memorization result is an existence theorem, not an empirical random-label test. It does not report generalization or chance-level test error for random labels. The convergence theorem uses a specialized initialization. The illustrative loss result is only a plot, with no numeric values stated in the text.

untested.parts: Chance-level classification test error and fitting random classification labels with unchanged standard architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Shuffled-pixel and independently permuted-pixel inputs; comparisons using the same networks and training settings across structured and unstructured inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error across a label-corruption sweep.
Effects of weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise.

record.verdict_notes: The random-label CIFAR-10 and ImageNet numbers are cited prior results. The paper's own Gaussian-input fitting result is explicitly stated in Section 4 and should not be dismissed merely because exact plot coordinates are unavailable. No scope limitation is inferred solely from sufficient theorem assumptions.

versions.untested_parts: The theorem states arbitrary real-valued labels can be fit up to arbitrary error, but does not report an experiment on completely random image labels, test error at chance, or unchanged standard training hyperparameters.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels or sweep over corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input fitting experiment.
No sweep over label corruption or measurement of test error as corruption increases.
No comparison of explicit regularization or data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
No measurement of learning order or comparison of real-label and random-label learning over training.

rows.subject: L-layer neural network (2.1)
rows.size_stated: Over-parameterization: N · log8 N = o(nL−2 nL−1); number of parameters between last two hidden layers is linear in N up to logarithmic factors.
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical memorization-capacity result: existence of parameters fitting any real-valued label vector up to arbitrarily small error.

conditions.value: smooth non-linear M-Lipschitz function with M′-Lipschitz derivative

rows.value: For every ε > 0, there exists θ such that ||FL(θ) − Y||₂² ≤ ε.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − C N e^(−c log² nL−1) − C e^(−c log² N); c and C numerical constants.
rows.note: The result is a theorem about existence of parameters for arbitrary real-valued labels, not a reported random-label image experiment; it does not state test error.
rows.check: This is an existence result, not evidence that training reaches the fitting parameters. Equation (4.1) bounds the unsquared Euclidean norm, not its square. Appendix G implements the construction with twice as many neurons in every hidden layer.

rows.subject: L-layer neural network (2.1)
rows.size_stated: Over-parameterization: N · log8 N = o(nL−2 nL−1); number of parameters between last two hidden layers is linear in N up to logarithmic factors.
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on least-squares loss from the duplicated-neuron initialization (4.2), with boosted final-layer variance γ = d³N² and a learning-rate upper bound.

conditions.value: (4.2), including duplicated hidden neurons and opposite final-layer weights

rows.measure: Least-squares training loss over gradient-descent steps.
rows.value: For all t ≥ 1, L(θt) ≤ (1 − cηγnL−2nL−1)^t L(θ0).
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − C N e^(−c log² nL−1) − C e^(−c log² N); c and C numerical constants.
rows.note: This is a convergence guarantee with a specially chosen initialization and stated learning-rate constraint, not unchanged standard hyperparameters.
rows.check: The theorem guarantees convergence to zero training loss for arbitrary suitably scaled labels; Gaussian inputs satisfy its data assumptions. Its guarantee requires smooth activations, sufficient over-parameterization, duplicated neurons, boosted output-weight variance and a constrained learning rate. It does not establish unchanged standard training settings.

rows.subject: 4-layer ReLU network
rows.size_stated: d = n1 = n2 = n3; width varied; plot describes parameter count at least linear in training-sample count.
rows.operation_detail: Illustrative loss experiment using Adam; inputs and targets sampled from standard Gaussian distributions; results averaged over 10 independent trials.
rows.measure: Training loss after gradient descent has converged.
rows.uncertainty: Plot averaged over 10 independent trials; no numerical interval stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: This illustrative regression experiment is not a random-label image experiment and does not provide extractable numeric loss values in the text.
rows.check: The accompanying text explicitly reports that loss falls from 1 to 0 when widths reach order sqrt(N), so the result is readable without extracting plot coordinates. This is Gaussian-input regression with Gaussian targets, trained using Adam and standard initialization, averaged over 10 trials. Narrower networks do not achieve zero loss.
